Chapter 2 — what locates algae within a survey year

Moorea 10 × 10 m lagoon grids, 2018–2024, fringing habitat dropped.

Design specification and results · families A–C (35 fits) plus the narrow-scope within-lagoon and paired-grid checks (S14, S15). The previous Gaussian analysis is preserved unaltered in chapter2_q1_by_year_lmer_no_fringing.html.

Scope of this document

One question: what locates algae within a survey year. Not what changes it between years, not what temperature does, not what happens on resurveyed grids — those are separate analyses and nothing here depends on them.

§1 fixes every rule the models ran under and the reasoning behind each one; §2 reports what they returned. The short version: algae on the hard bottom is lower where coral is higher, lower where it is deeper, and higher where relief is greater — each significant in all seven years, and nothing else in the model manages that. Two reading conventions decide how every coefficient below is interpreted, and one of them has changed — worth fixing in mind first:

Depth sign, and the 2020 season

Depth is now metres below the surface, positive downward. A positive depth coefficient therefore means deeper grids hold more algae, which is what a reader assumes it means. The raw layer is bathymetry, negative below the surface, and it is negated before scaling.

This reverses the sign of the depth coefficient against every earlier Chapter 2 output, where a positive β meant shallower. The relationship in the data has not changed; only its presentation has. Since algae is in fact higher in shallow water here, depth should now report as negative — if you are comparing against an old table, negate one of them first.

2020 was surveyed in Sep–Oct, not May–Jun. It stays in as its own per-year model, marked, but is excluded from every cross-year direction or consistency summary, which are computed on the six May–Jun years. Where a summary says n = 6, 2020 is out.

1 · Design & data lock

Every rule the models ran under, and the reasoning behind each one. Rows marked carried forward are unchanged from the original analysis; rows marked change are the corrections argued for below. Every rule here was settled before the fits ran; where a rule has a stated fallback (spatial convergence, zero handling, the nudge) the fallback and its trigger were settled too, so nothing was left to be decided after seeing a result.

Zero handlingModelled directly by the ordered Beta — no nudge, no zero-inflationGenuinely algae-free grids exist, so the zeros are neither artefacts to be squeezed away nor a separate process to be split off. A ziformula would redefine every coefficient as an effect conditional on algae being present, which is not the chapter’s claim. The Smithson–Verkuilen squeeze avoids that but places a zero at 0.5/n, which moves with sample size — the same ecological zero would sit at logit −7.99 in 2019 and −8.96 in 2023. In a design that compares coefficients across years that is a confound, not a nuisance. Ordered Beta treats 0 and 1 as real outcomes via cutpoints and keeps the coefficients unconditional. The squeezed Beta becomes the reported sensitivity.change
Spatial term(1 | Lagoon) + exp(pos3 + 0 | Lagoon), with pos3 on a 100 m knot latticeWas a single island-wide field, which can imitate a smooth island-scale gradient and compete with depth, offshore ratio, distance to pass and nutrient. The field is anchored on knots, not on raw centroids: at full 10 m resolution it is not identifiable, taking 27 minutes and returning unusable standard errors. Snapping pos3 to a 100 m lattice changes only which grids share a spatial random effect — no response or predictor is averaged, and all rows are kept. Refitted at 150 / 100 / 75 / 50 m; the fitted range comes out at 158–1,069 m, comfortably above the lattice. See §1.4.change

All previous results have been removed from this document rather than shown with caveats, because these rules change the likelihood, the row set, the spatial term and two predictors — a coefficient fitted under the old rules is not comparable to one fitted under these. The full previous analysis is preserved in chapter2_q1_by_year_lmer_no_fringing.html. §1.1–§1.4 set out what changed and why; §2 reports what those fits returned.

1.1 · The response, and what its shape requires

Every model here is a model of one quantity: algae_std_A_CHS, the algae share of hard bottom. Its distribution decides which likelihood is defensible, so it is worth looking at before any coefficient.

Left: the response with a Gaussian of the same mean and standard deviation overlaid. The shaded band left of zero is the probability that Gaussian assigns to negative algae cover. Centre and right: the same grid-years split by how many photographs the grid received.

Three properties of the response, and the change each one forces

1 — It is bounded and skewed, so the likelihood changes. The response lives on [0, 1] with a median of 0.070 against a mean of 0.133 across all grid-years at ≥ 5 photos, and 0.077 against 0.135 once the ≥ 20 rule below is applied. A Gaussian fitted to it places real probability mass below zero, which is why the dashed curve crosses the boundary. A Beta likelihood with a logit link cannot produce an impossible value and has the right variance shape for a proportion. Eight grid-years also sit at exactly 1.0, so both boundaries are occupied.

2 — The variance is not constant, so the weighting changes. Spread falls monotonically with effort — 0.190, 0.174, 0.167, 0.144, 0.122 across the five effort bins. A Gaussian assumes one common residual variance and therefore weights a 20-photo grid exactly as heavily as a 2,560-photo grid. Modelling dispersion on log(n_photos) tells the model which grids to trust. It is logged because effort has strongly diminishing returns — 20 to 40 photos changes reliability far more than 500 to 520 — and because effort still spans a 128-fold range after the threshold.

3 — Many zeros are non-detections, so the sample changes. A grid photographed fewer than 15 times records zero algae 38.6 % of the time; a grid photographed 100 or more times records zero only 2.7 % of the time. Most low-effort zeros mean we did not look enough to find the algae. Raising the minimum effort removes those without pretending the remaining zeros are artefacts.

Under the adopted rule the response looks like this, with the Beta component of the ordered-Beta model drawn over the top:

The green curve is a method-of-moments Beta fitted to the values strictly inside (0, 1) and rescaled by their share, so it describes only the continuous part. The model itself is ordered Beta: it keeps the exact zeros as real outcomes rather than nudging them. The y-axis is clipped so the curve stays readable; the true height of the first bin is annotated.

What the threshold costs, and why the remaining zeros are left alone

Raising the minimum from 5 to 20 photos cuts the zero spike from 13.2 % to 9.6 % while barely touching the shape of the rest of the distribution. It is a straight trade of sample size against measurement quality:

Minimum photosgrid-years kept% of currentexact zerossmallest year
533,141100 %13.2 %1,873
1031,57795 %11.8 %1,732
20 ← proposed28,42486 %9.6 %1,486
3025,20076 %7.7 %1,195
5016,33249 %5.5 %289

“Smallest year” is the number of grid-years left in the thinnest survey year, which is what limits how far the threshold can go.

At 20 photos 86 % of grid-years are kept. Going to 50 halves the dataset and leaves the thinnest year too small to carry nine predictors, which is why 20–30 was the usable window. Twenty is settled; 5 and 30, plus a no-dispersion arm, are the S13 sensitivity in §2.4.

The remaining zeros are kept as real, and the likelihood is chosen to accept them. After the threshold, between 6 % and 18 % of grid-years still read exactly zero depending on the year, and a Beta distribution cannot produce an exact zero. There are three ways out and only one of them fits this chapter:

  • Zero-inflation splits the zeros into a separate process. Declined: it redefines every coefficient as an effect conditional on algae being present, which is a different claim from the one this chapter makes.
  • Squeeze the zeros inside the interval (Smithson & Verkuilen 2006, y′ = (y(n − 1) + 0.5) / n). This is the conventional fix and it keeps the coefficients unconditional, but it was designed for a handful of boundary values, not for one grid in ten. It also places a zero at 0.5/n, so the value depends on how many grids were surveyed that year: an identical algae-free grid lands at logit −7.99 in 2019 and −8.96 in 2023, purely because 2023 has more rows. Since the entire design compares coefficients across years, that is a confound rather than a nuisance.
  • Ordered Beta (Kubinec 2022) treats 0 and 1 as genuine outcomes through cutpoints. No nudge, nothing that moves with sample size, and the coefficients stay unconditional. This is what the models use.

The choice is not cosmetic, and it was checked rather than assumed. Fitting both on 2019 and 2022: no significant coefficient changes sign, and depth, max relief and VRM are stable — but coral’s magnitude moves by up to 46 %, herbivore changes significance in both years, and the ordered Beta returns slightly tighter standard errors throughout, since it is not spending effort accommodating an artificial spike. Because §1.5 makes coral’s magnitude the headline claim, that difference lands directly on the chapter’s main result. The squeezed Beta is refitted as the reported sensitivity so the comparison is on the record.

The obvious objection to all of this is “why not just fit a linear model?” It deserves an answer on these data rather than an appeal to principle, so the 2019 model was fitted three ways — Gaussian, Beta with the squeeze, and ordered Beta — on the same 1,475 grid-years, with the same nine predictors and a lagoon intercept only, so that nothing but the likelihood differs.

The two things this table settles

1 — The conclusions do not depend on the likelihood. Gaussian and ordered Beta agree on sign for eight of nine predictors and on significance for eight of nine. The lone exception is nutrient, which the Gaussian leaves at +0.011 (n.s.) and the ordered Beta returns as −0.191 (p < 0.05) — and §1.5 shows nutrient is not separably identified from spatial structure in any case, so it is not a coefficient this chapter reports as a finding. Nothing in the headline result rests on the choice of likelihood, and it should not be defended as though it does.

2 — The linear model is nevertheless not available. Fitted to these data the Gaussian predicts negative algae cover for 226 of the 1,475 grids — 15.3 % — with fitted values running from −0.119 to 0.452. Its residual SD is 0.089 against a mean of 0.12, so even at the average grid its 95 % prediction interval reaches −0.054. A model of cover that returns negative cover for one grid in seven cannot be defended, however well its signs happen to agree. The ordered Beta’s fitted values run from 0.007 to 0.577 — inside the possible range by construction, not by luck.

So the case for ordered Beta is not that it finds different answers. It is that it is the version of this analysis that cannot return an impossible number. It is also a strict generalisation: when a boundary is unoccupied its cutpoint runs to infinity and the fit collapses back to a plain Beta, which is exactly what happens to the upper cutpoint here (k₂ = 127).

interpretationWhat the coefficients mean in plain units — worked through

A logit-scale coefficient cannot be read as it stands, so each one is converted into change in algae share per 2 SD of the predictor. The response is algae as a share of the hard bottom in a grid, so a share of 0.119 means 11.9 % of that grid's hard bottom is algae.

Worked example: what “depth −0.064” actually says

Take depth in 2019. Its coefficient is −0.064 share units per 2 SD, and in that year 2 SD of depth is 0.83 m — less than a metre.

StepValue
Average grid in 20190.119  =  11.9 % of hard bottom is algae
Move it 0.83 m deepershare changes by −0.064
Result 0.119 − 0.064 = 0.055  =  5.5 % of hard bottom

So it is a subtraction, not a percentage of a percentage. The algae share falls from 11.9 % to 5.5 % of the hard bottom. That is what “6.4 percentage points” means.

The two readings people mix up:

  • Percentage points (correct here). 11.9 % − 6.4 % = 5.5 %. The gap between two percentages.
  • Percent, i.e. relative change (not what the coefficient is). That would be 11.9 % × (1−0.064) = 11.1 %, a trivial change. Wrong by a factor of ten.

If you do want the relative statement, compute it from the two endpoints: 5.5 against 11.9 is a 54 % reduction — under a metre of extra depth is associated with roughly half the algae. Both statements describe the same result; only the first is what the coefficient directly gives you.

Why the textbook shortcut is not used, and what replaced it

The usual quick conversion is β × p̄(1 − p̄). That is the slope of the logistic curve at a single point, so it approximates a curve with a straight line, and the approximation decays as the coefficient gets larger and the move runs further along the curve.

On this fit the drift is not negligible. The shortcut overstates depth by 45 % (−0.093 against a true −0.064) and understates the between-lagoon nutrient term by 25 %. An earlier version of this document reported the shortcut values and described them as agreeing with the exact form; on the current fit they do not, and the amber rows above are where they part company by 20 % or more.

Every share-unit figure quoted here is therefore the exact average marginal effect: shift every grid by 2 SD, recompute its expected share, average the change.

share_per_2sd = mean( E[y | η + β] ) − mean( E[y | η] )

No approximation, and it stays correct however large the coefficient.

interpretationHow the predicted share is computed, and the trap in predict()

Predictions are plotted on the data scale with every other predictor held at its mean:

Blue is the expected algae share including the zeros, bounded in [0, 1] by construction. Orange dashed is what predict(type = "response") returns. Grey points are the observed data in deciles. The depth panel is the calibration check — the observed means track the fitted curve. The other three scatter more because the grey points are raw marginal means while the curve is a partial effect holding the other predictors fixed, so they are not expected to coincide.

The two curves are different quantities, and only one of them is the expected share. An ordered Beta grid can land in three places, governed by the linear predictor η and two cutpoints k₁ < k₂:

P(y = 0)      = 1 − logit⁻¹(η − k₁)      # bare: no algae at all
P(0 < y < 1)  =     logit⁻¹(η − k₁) − logit⁻¹(η − k₂)
P(y = 1)      =     logit⁻¹(η − k₂)      # wholly algae

E[y | 0 < y < 1] = logit⁻¹(η)          # mean of the Beta part alone

The expected share has to average over all three outcomes, weighting each by how likely it is:

E[y] = P(0 < y < 1) × logit⁻¹(η)  +  P(y = 1) × 1  +  P(y = 0) × 0
     ↳ this is the BLUE line, and what ch2_q1_expected_share() returns

predict(type = "response") = logit⁻¹(η)
     ↳ this is the ORANGE line: the middle piece only, ignoring the weights

Why orange sits above blue. logit−1(η) answers a narrower question — given that a grid has some algae but is not wholly covered, how much does it have? It never asks whether the grid has any algae at all. Blue multiplies that by the probability the grid is not bare, so wherever bare grids are likely, blue is pulled down and orange is not.

On the 2019 fit, with k₁ = −4.50 and k₂ = 126.6:

QuantityValue
P(y = 0), averaged over grids0.18118 % of grids predicted bare
P(y = 1), averaged over grids0.000k₂ ran off, so this term vanishes
mean logit−1(η) — orange0.1264 
mean E[y] — blue0.1186 
observed mean share0.1207 blue lands within 0.002 of it

Because P(y = 1) is zero here, the second equation collapses to E[y] = P(0 < y < 1) × logit−1(η) — blue is simply orange scaled down, grid by grid, by the chance the grid is not bare.

The practical consequence

Reporting predict(type = "response") as an expected share overstates it by 6.6 % on this fit, and the error is not constant — it grows wherever bare grids are common, so it distorts the shape of a fitted curve, not just its level.

Anything reported as an expected share therefore goes through ch2_q1_expected_share() in chapter2_q1_refit_helpers.R, which reassembles the three pieces above. Its output reproduces the observed 2019 mean to within 0.0021, which is the calibration check. The same trap caught ch2_q1_share_units(), which used mean(logit−1(η)) as its baseline until it was corrected.

Nutrient — where the variable comes from, and why it cannot be a within-year driver

This was checked at source rather than inferred from the fits, because a variable behaving as oddly as nutrient does invites the suspicion that it was built wrongly. It was not. It is doing exactly what its pipeline was written to do, and the limits are in the underlying survey.

nutrient_allYear_percent_n_may comes from 3_nutrient_data/N_summary.csv: 190 point samples around Moorea (171 with a usable May value), inverse-distance interpolated at 25 m and averaged within each grid polygon by 9_nutrientDat_generator_grid.R. Three consequences follow, and all three are properties of the survey rather than of the code:

  • It is one snapshot, not a time series. The file carries Jan, May and July columns from a single sampling campaign. Zero of 16,496 grid cells take a different nutrient value in any year, which is why the column is named allYear. It therefore cannot explain year-to-year change in algae, and any apparent nutrient effect is a statement about where, never when.
  • Its real resolution is hundreds of metres. Median spacing between neighbouring sample points is 385 m. The median grid sits 163 m from the nearest actual measurement; only 26 % are within 100 m and 7 % are more than 500 m away. Everything between the points is interpolation. This is why the neighbour correlation in F2 is 1.00: at 100 m the surface is by construction smooth, so that diagnostic is partly measuring the interpolator rather than the reef.
  • The season is a choice, and the seasons disagree. May correlates only r = 0.46 with January and r = 0.42 with July at the same points. “Nutrient” here means the May snapshot specifically, not a stable nutrient regime, and picking a different column would give a materially different predictor.

What is not wrong with it. The layer does vary in space within a year, and it varies at both scales: averaged over years, 33.5 % of its variance is within lagoons (range 21.7–46.5 %) and the rest is between them. So there is real contrast for a within-year model to work with. The missing dimension is time, not space.

What follows for the chapter. The variable stays in the model, but not because the model needs it. The direct test in §1.3 is unambiguous: dropping all three smooth predictors moves coral, depth and max relief by at most 0.253 SE (median 0.09 SE) and leaves their standard errors unchanged to two decimal places. Numerically the choice is nearly free, so it has to be made on other grounds:

  • Removing it would be selection on the result. Nutrient was in the a priori predictor set as an ecological hypothesis. Dropping it after seeing that its pooled coefficient was unstable is exactly the stepwise selection §1.2 rules out for every other predictor; there is no principle that would justify it here and not there.
  • Split, it returns a clean answer rather than an unusable one. That is the point of §1.3. The between-lagoon term is positive in all seven years and significant in five (2019–2023, β 1.68–2.58); the within-lagoon term is null in all seven, with the sign flipping five times positive to two negative. A reported null is a result. Silence is not.

What it still cannot do. Not one of 16,496 grid cells changes value between years, so the layer cannot address whether changing nutrients change algae — the question most readers will assume is being asked. The between-lagoon association it does support rests on 11 lagoons, not 28,424 grid-years, and 11 lagoons differ in far more than their %N. Write it up as lagoons with higher May %N tend to have more algae, on eleven lagoons, with no within-lagoon association and no ability to separate nutrients from anything else that varies between lagoons. Testing a nutrient hypothesis properly needs a time-varying product; this layer cannot do it however it is modelled.

Herbivore biomass — why it stays in, and the one check the late years need

Herbivore biomass is 41.4 % missing and is not imputed, so complete.cases removes those rows outright. That single variable is what takes the analysis from 28,424 grid-years to 16,663. The pooled figure is misleading though: no lagoon-year is entirely unsurveyed, and the gap is almost purely temporal.

Imbalance is the mean offshore ratio of grids with a herbivore value minus those without, in SD of that year. Positive means the fish-surveyed grids sit further toward the crest.

2018–2021 are essentially complete at 98–100 % and need no special handling. The gap is confined to 2022–2024, at 37–43 %, and the cause is known: benthic imaging was scaled up with an ROV from 2022 while fish counts still require a human observer, so benthic coverage grew while fish coverage did not. The data are therefore missing by design, not missing for reasons connected to algae — what decides whether a grid has a fish value is where a diver could work.

Missing is not zero here, and the column proves it. 251 of the 16,667 herbivore-surveyed grid-years (1.5 %) record exactly 0 g m−2 of biomass and exactly 0 density: someone looked and found no herbivores. Because a real zero is recorded as a zero, an NA can only mean nobody surveyed that grid. Leaving those rows missing is correct.

The one check the late years need. In 2023 and 2024 the surveyed grids sit +0.29 to +0.35 SD further offshore, so the question is whether the geography coefficients are a property of the reef or of which third of the grids got a fish survey. Fit the model without herbivore twice: once on the grids that have a fish survey, once on all grids. The formula is identical, so the only difference is which grids are included and any movement in the offshore-ratio coefficient is attributable to the sample alone. Herbivory stays in the reported model either way.

Say plainly what family A therefore estimates. Because herbivore biomass is in the formula and is never imputed, family A is fitted on fish-surveyed grids by construction. In 2018–2021 that is 98–100 % of the grid-years and the distinction is immaterial. In 2022–2024 it is 37–43 %, so the late-year estimand is what locates algae among grids a diver could work, not among all photographed reef. That is a real restriction on the reported result, not something family B removes — B diagnoses whether the restriction moves the geography, and it is the same restriction either way.

How the pair is read, which was decided before it ran. The comparison is on the geography terms. 2018–2021 fix the reference: those years have almost identical row sets, so whatever separation they produce is measurement noise and sets the bar the late years must beat. 2022–2023 separate on depth magnitude (2.4–2.5 SD) while the sign holds, so those two years’ depth coefficients are reported with the fish-survey restriction stated and are not pooled with 2018–2021 as the same estimand. Family A is not refitted without herbivore to escape the problem: dropping a predictor to widen the sample changes what every other coefficient means. Detail in §1.6 / S6 and §2.2.

Spear density — the imputation was doing real damage, so it moves to its own analysis

Spear density is measured by following a subset of island fishers. Where they went there is a value; where they did not, the field is empty and is currently recoded to zero — for 61.7 % of grids. Unlike herbivore biomass, no genuine measured zero exists anywhere in the column (the smallest observed value is 0.01), so there is nothing in the data to justify reading an absence as a zero.

That would be a tolerable approximation if the tracked fishers had covered the island evenly. They did not, and the consequence is measurable:

Correlationnr
Spear vs algae — as currently modelled (NA→0)n = 28,424-0.055
Spear vs algae — real measurements onlyn = 10,885-0.029
No-data flag vs algae — contains no fishing informationn = 28,424+0.133
No-data flag vs % MPAn = 28,424+0.180
No-data flag vs offshore ration = 28,424-0.226

All correlations on the primary modelling set at ≥ 20 photos — all 11 lagoons, since this is a diagnosis of what spear was doing inside the primary model. That is why 10,885 grid-years appear here but only 10,228 below: the fishing analysis reinstates the Ch1 lagoon filter, and the primary model no longer does. The “no-data flag” is simply 1 where spear was never measured — it contains no fishing information at all.

The imputed variable carries a stronger signal than the real measurements do. The bare fact of having no data correlates with algae at +0.133, while the actual spear measurements correlate with algae at only −0.029 where they exist. So most of what the model reads as a fishing effect is a map of where the trackers went, not a map of fishing pressure.

It also contaminates a predictor you care about. The unmeasured grids are disproportionately inside protected water — 69.3 % of MPA grids lack spear data against 51.6 % outside — so 39.5 % of all grids are simultaneously “spear = 0 (imputed)” and “inside MPA”. A negative spear coefficient and a positive MPA coefficient would then be partly the same contrast, measured twice.

Why the obvious fix does not work. Recoding to a simple fished / not-fished binary makes it worse, not better: that binary is the coverage map, so it isolates the artefact instead of removing it.

Decision: spear is dropped from the primary model, and fishing is analysed separately on the 10,228 grid-years where it was genuinely measured, keeping the Ch1 filter. The MPA coefficient stops sharing a contrast with an imputation artefact, and what the primary model loses is small: under the previous fits spear reached significance in 2 of 7 years, and on the evidence above that signal was largely the coverage map rather than fishing.

What the primary model can then say about human use is narrower, and should be worded that way. MPA status is complete and clean and stays in every fit, but it is protection on paper, not extraction. It is a zoning contrast, not a measure of fishing pressure, and it cannot stand in for one. Island-wide statements about fishing are no longer available from family A at all; the only fishing claim this chapter can make is family C’s, scoped to the tracked grids.

Measured grid-years at ≥ 20 photos, and whether spear effort varies within a lagoon-year rather than only between lagoons.

The separate analysis is narrower but better identified. All seven years are fittable, and spear effort varies within the lagoon in 45 of the 47 lagoon-years on the measured subset, across two to three orders of magnitude. That means a fishing gradient can be estimated with lagoon held fixed, which is what turns it into a dose–response result rather than a between-lagoon comparison that anything could confound. It buys identification by giving up reach: it is a better test of a smaller question.

This is the one analysis that keeps the Ch1 lagoon filter. That filter exists because Chapter 1 could not see fishing in Tiahura, Papetoai and west Pihaena — which is exactly the limitation that binds here, and exactly the limitation that does not bind a model with no fishing term. So family C runs inside the Ch1 universe: 13,597 complete grid-years, of which 6,241 carry a real spear measurement.

But the fished subset is not a random slice of that universe, so each year is fitted twice. Those 6,241 grids sit +0.48 SD further offshore than the unmeasured ones, +0.38 SD further from a pass, −0.13 SD on MPA coverage — and, decisively, −0.28 SD on algae itself. The fished grids already carry less algae before a single term is estimated. Fitting spear on that subset alone would confound the fishing effect with the act of selecting a lower-algae part of the lagoon. So each year gets a pair: the same specification on the same rows, once without spear and once with it. The first fit absorbs whatever the subset is; only the difference between them is read as fishing.

What the pair does and does not fix. Both fits sit on the same selected 6,241 rows, so the pair removes the risk of attributing the subset’s own character to spear — it does not make the subset representative. The estimand is the effect of additional spearfishing effort among grids the tracked fishers visited. Generalising it to the 61.7 % nobody tracked requires an assumption the data cannot test, and the chapter should not make one.

MPA stays in the fishing models. The 39.5 % overlap above is between MPA and the missingness flag, and that flag is gone once the analysis is restricted to measured grids. Among those grids the two are effectively independent: median spear effort is 0.42 inside the MPA and 0.43 outside, and the correlation between MPA status and effort is r = −0.024. Among tracked grids the boundary is not tracking effort, which is itself why the two terms are worth keeping apart — MPA is protection on paper, spear is extraction in fact. Four of the nine lagoons contain both MPA states, so the contrast is estimable within lagoon.

What it answers: among the areas this fleet fished, holding lagoon, depth, coral and geography constant, do grids that received more spearfishing effort carry more algae? What it cannot answer is anything about the 61.7 % nobody tracked. The claim moved from an island-wide assertion the data cannot support to a scoped one it can. Spear is not distinguishable from zero in any year (§2.3). The thin year is 2022, at 504 complete rows across five lagoons; it is reported but not leaned on.

1.3 · The three smooth predictors, and why they enter split

Nutrient, inside-MPA and distance to pass are the three predictors flagged in §1.5 as too spatially smooth to be separated from the lagoon spatial field. This section records what was done about them, because it is a change from how they were previously fitted and the reason is not obvious from the model formula alone.

Changing the knot spacing does not fix it. That was the first thing tried. In the pooled form — each smooth predictor entering as a single term, as it did before the split below — nutrient ran from −0.276 to +0.151 across spacings within 2019 alone, a sign reversal from nothing but the lattice, and distance to pass did the same within 2023. Coarser knots leave more for the predictors to explain, finer knots leave less, and the coefficient tracks that choice rather than the reef. No spacing is the right one, because spacing is not the problem.

The split is what contains it. Once each variable enters as a lagoon mean plus a within-lagoon deviation, the spacing no longer moves the between-lagoon part in any year, and the flipping is confined to within-lagoon components that are never separable from zero anyway. The rebuilt sensitivity in §1.4 shows the post-split picture across all seven years.

What the split actually does — the same rows, written two ways

The split is the primary specification, not a sensitivity: every nutrient, MPA and distance-to-pass coefficient reported in §2 comes from it. The pooled form is kept only as the primary_pooledsmooth check. The figure below works the arithmetic on real 2019 rows.

Built from the exact rows the 2019 primary model was fitted on (05xc_q1_split_illustration.R). Nutrient is shown because it is the clearest case; MPA and distance to pass are split the same way.

Panel 1 is the whole mechanism. A grid in Teavaro with 0.446 %N becomes 0.423 (its lagoon’s mean) plus +0.023 (how far above that lagoon it sits). Nothing is added and nothing is discarded — x = x_btw + x_wth exactly. The model now has two columns where it had one, and each answers a question the other cannot:

  • _btw is identical for every grid in a lagoon. It can only answer do high-nutrient lagoons have more algae? — and its real sample size is the number of lagoons, seven that year, not 1,475 grids.
  • _wth is what is left after each lagoon is centred, so it is free of any difference between lagoons. It answers inside one lagoon, do the higher-nutrient grids have more algae?

Panel 2 shows why one coefficient could not do both. Two-thirds of the variation in nutrient is between lagoons and one third is inside them. A pooled predictor averages across that divide, producing a single number that is neither answer, weighted by an accident of how the sampling happened to fall.

Panel 3 is the payoff. Separated, the two halves behave completely differently. The between-lagoon term is positive in all seven years and significant in five. The within-lagoon term is significant in none, with its sign flipping five to two. The pooled coefficient was a blend of a real lagoon-scale association and a within-lagoon null — which is exactly why it moved whenever the knot spacing changed.

The problem is that one coefficient was being asked two different questions

About two-thirds of the variation in each of these three sits between lagoons rather than within them. So a single pooled coefficient was mixing two questions that have different answers, different sample sizes and different susceptibility to confounding:

  • Do lagoons with more of it have more algae? A between-lagoon contrast, resting on 6–11 lagoons, and confounded with everything else that differs between lagoons.
  • Within one lagoon, do grids with more of it have more algae? A within-lagoon contrast, resting on thousands of grids, and free of between-lagoon confounding.

The lagoon random effect competes for the first question and not the second, which is exactly why the pooled estimate moved whenever the spatial term was re-tuned.

Within-lagoon share of each predictor's variance. A value of 0.33 means one third of the variation is within lagoons and two thirds is between them.

That makes this a free choice, to be settled on interpretability rather than forced by confounding.

Shift is |estimatealt − estimatefull| in standard errors of the full model, maximised over coral, depth and max relief. Script: 05za_q1_smooth_predictor_decision.R.

The options, and why the split was taken:

OptionWhy it was or was not taken
Keep pooled (what was there)One coefficient per predictor, as fitted until now.
The coefficient is a blend of a between-lagoon and a within-lagoon contrast in unknown proportion. All three flip sign across years and two flip from nothing but the knot spacing. Nothing can be reported from it.
Drop all threeFit the six identified predictors only.
Defensible — it moves the firm three by at most 0.25 SE — but it throws away a real between-lagoon nutrient result, and it invites the reasonable question of why three ecologically motivated variables were omitted.
Within component onlyKeep the deviation from the lagoon mean; let the lagoon random effect absorb the rest.
Statistically clean, and the within coefficient is unbiased for the within question. But it silently discards the between-lagoon variation instead of reporting it, which for nutrient is where the entire signal lives.
Split into between + within
ADOPTED		Each smooth predictor enters twice: its lagoon mean, and the deviation from that mean.
Keeps every predictor in the model so the “adjusted for” claim holds, asks the two questions separately instead of blending them, and makes the true sample size behind each visible. This is what turns three unusable coefficients into one clear result and two clear nulls.

What splitting actually recovers — one result and two nulls

This is the argument for the change. The pooled column is what was being fitted before; the two columns beneath each are the same variable asked the two questions separately.

Nutrient has a real and consistent signal, and it is entirely between lagoons. The between-lagoon coefficient is positive in all seven years and significant in five; the within-lagoon coefficient is null in all seven. Pooling them averaged a strong signal with a null and produced the sign-flipping mess in the top row. Lagoons scoring higher on the May %N surface carry more algae; where a grid sits relative to its own lagoon's mean tells you nothing.

The MPA effect is cleanly null within lagoons. Its within-lagoon coefficient never approaches significance in any year. Its between-lagoon coefficient is significant in four years but flips sign, which is the signature of a lagoon-level confound rather than a protection effect — MPAs are not placed at random, so lagoons with more protection differ in many other ways. This independently confirms the earlier within-lagoon test.

Distance to pass has nothing either way, flipping sign in both components. It stays in the model for adjustment but supports no claim.

An unplanned benefit. Under the pooled specification 2024 could not be fitted with the lagoon-grouped spatial field at all: its lagoon intercept variance collapsed to sd = 0.001, the covariance matrix returned NaN, every standard error came back missing, and the year had to fall back to a single island-wide field. Under the split it converges normally, so all seven years now carry the same spatial structure with no fallbacks. That is what you would expect if the pooled smooth terms had been competing with the lagoon effect for the same variation, and it is independent support for the diagnosis above.

Ordered Beta, 100 m knots, logit scale. *** p < 0.001, ** p < 0.01, * p < 0.05.

Three caveats that must travel with any between-lagoon coefficient

  1. The sample size is lagoons, not grids. Every between-lagoon coefficient rests on 6–11 points, not on 28,424 grid-years. It is reported at that resolution and should be read as a lagoon-scale association.
  2. For nutrient, the seven years are not seven replications. The nutrient layer is static (§1.2): its lagoon means are identical in every year. Seven consistent estimates are seven looks at the same eleven numbers, so consistency across years is not independent evidence here, and it should not be presented as if it were.
  3. The between-lagoon components are not cleanly separable from each other. At the lagoon level nutrient and distance to pass correlate at r = −0.53 across the eleven lagoons. With three between-terms and eleven lagoons, the nutrient result should be read as “lagoons high on this surface have more algae”, not as an isolated nutrient mechanism.

1.4 · The models that were fitted

This is the specification the results in §2 were produced under, written out so those tables can be read against it. Three families of model, 35 fits, sharing the same likelihood, scaling and spatial structure — they differ only in which rows and which terms they use, which is what makes them comparable. The narrow-scope checks in §2.5 are additional and are not among these 35.

Shaded marks any fit standing on six lagoons or fewer — 2021 and 2022 throughout, and family C also in 2019. Family B fits the same lagoons in both arms of every pair, so its contrast is rows within fixed lagoons.

Columns A and B · fish-surveyed are identical, and that is not a duplication. Herbivore biomass is in family A’s formula and is never imputed, so complete-case deletion drops exactly the grids without a fish survey: family A is fitted on the fish-surveyed subset, by construction rather than by choice. The columns are kept apart because the two are different models — A reports coefficients, B is the diagnostic that varies the row set against B · all rows to show what that deletion costs. The gap between the second and third columns is the whole point of family B, and in 2023 it is 9,016 rows against 3,895.

Why this is stated rather than left implicit. The spatial term estimates a variance and a range per lagoon, and (1 | Lagoon) is a random intercept over the same levels. In 2021 and 2022 that is six groups carrying roughly 1,400 rows. Six is a thin basis for a random intercept and a demanding one for six independent fields, so those two years are the ones most likely to hit the fallback described below, and their spatial ranges should be read with the least confidence. 2018 is the only year that fits all eleven.

Family A, written out:

algae_std_A_CHS ~ coral_std_A_CHS + herb_biomass
                + depth_m_below + maxRel + vrm + offshore_ratio
                + min_dist_to_pass_btw + min_dist_to_pass_wth    # split, see §1.3
                + mpa_inside_btw      + mpa_inside_wth
                + nutrient_allYear_btw + nutrient_allYear_wth
                + (1 | Lagoon) + exp(pos3 + 0 | Lagoon)   # pos3 = centroid snapped to a 100 m lattice

family      = ordbeta(link = "logit")   # glmmTMB >= 1.1.7
dispformula = ~ log(n_photos)
data        = grids with n_photos >= 20, no lagoon filter,
              complete cases on all nine predictors  (herbivore binds)
              _btw = lagoon mean, _wth = deviation from it; x = _btw + _wth, nothing dropped
              one model per survey year  (6-11 lagoons present, by year)

Families B and C reuse this exactly. B removes herb_biomass and swaps the row set; C adds spearDensity, restricts to the measured rows and reinstates the Ch1 lagoon filter.

What is deliberately not changing

One model per survey year. Years are not pooled and no year random effect is introduced. The question is what locates algae within a survey year, and keeping the years separate is what makes the consistency argument across years meaningful rather than assumed.

Every predictor stays in, together. No stepwise selection and no dropping of null predictors. Herbivore biomass in particular stays in.

Gelman 2-SD scaling stays. Under a logit link the coefficients become log-odds rather than share points, so every reported effect needs converting back to share units the way the coral coefficient already is in F1. This is a reporting obligation, not an obstacle.

The conversion rule. A logit slope is not a constant effect on shares — how many share points a coefficient is worth depends on where you sit on the curve. The rule for this chapter is the average marginal effect per 2 SD: move every grid 2 SD along the predictor, recompute its expected share, and average the change.

share_per_2sd = mean( E[y | η + β] ) − mean( E[y | η] )

Two details matter and both were got wrong at first, so they are stated explicitly. E[y] is the full expected share including the exact zeros, not logit−1(η) — see the trap in §1.1. And the exact difference is used rather than the textbook shortcut β × p̄(1 − p̄), which is a straight-line approximation to a curve and overstates the depth effect by 45 % on the 2019 fit.

Since the expected share is around 0.12, the same log-odds coefficient is worth roughly a ninth as much in share points, so a coefficient that looks large on the log-odds scale can be small on the reef. Every converted number must carry the year it was evaluated in, because a year with more algae converts the same coefficient into a larger share effect. The conversion is for reading the magnitude; significance is always read on the fitted scale.

2020 stays in, still flagged as a Sep–Oct survey among May–Jun ones, and still excluded from the cross-year direction summaries.

The spatial field is anchored on 100 m knots — what that means, and why

pos3 above is not the raw grid centroid. It is the centroid snapped onto a 100 m lattice. This is the one specification choice in §1.4 that was forced by the data rather than chosen on principle, so it is set out in full.

What a knot is, in one paragraph

The model carries a term for everything that was not measured but still varies across space — currents, sediment, disturbance history. Call it the background. The model has to estimate that background, and it cannot give every point its own value, because that would be as many unknowns as there are observations. So it is told: estimate one background value inside each box of a given size. The corners of those boxes are the knots, and the box size is the only thing being chosen. Knot spacing is therefore just how sharply the background is allowed to bend.

It does not change the resolution of the data. Every 10 × 10 m grid cell remains its own row, with its own algae value and its own nine predictors. Nothing is averaged, merged or dropped; the row counts are identical under every spacing tested. The only thing coarsened is the address the background term is indexed by.

Top: the black curve is the real background, which is unknowable. Each coloured staircase is what the model can represent at that knot spacing — one value per box. Bottom: the same 1,475 grid cells of Maatea in 2019 in all four panels, coloured by the background the model actually inferred, with the knot boxes drawn on. Left to right the map gains detail.

resolutionThe other half of the confusion: what knots do not touch

The same model and the same rows throughout. A typical 100 m knot covers nine grid cells, and 13 of the 143 knots in 2019 still hold a single cell on their own. The zoom also shows why the raw field failed: the surveys run as narrow, near-collinear tracks with hundreds of metres of open water between them, which is not the geometry needed to support one independent anchor per grid.

The raw-centroid field is not slow — it does not work.

Family A fits, timed. The raw-centroid row is not a timing failure: fitting family C 2018 (n = 1,116, 202 distinct positions in its largest lagoon) that way ran 27 minutes and returned pdHess = FALSE, so it produced no usable standard errors and the pipeline discarded it and fell back to an island-wide field. Every knotted fit converged. Across the full plan this is the difference between roughly a day of compute yielding mostly fallbacks, and about fifteen minutes yielding the specified model.

Why 100 m, given that all four spacings converge

Because the choice is not really computational. Whatever detail the background traces is taken away from predictors that vary just as smoothly — the field and the predictor are competing to explain the same pattern. So family A was refitted at every spacing in every year, which separates the predictors that survive that competition from the ones that do not:

PredictorYears where the sign
flips across spacings		Worst spread
within one year, log-odds		Years significant
at all spacings

Nutrient · between0 of 70.2735 / 7

All seven years × four spacings, refitted by the pipeline itself (primary_knot<m> rows in primary_fixed_effects), on the split specification adopted in §1.3. “Worst spread” is the largest gap between the highest and lowest estimate any single year produced across its spacings.

There are three behaviours here, not two, and the distinction governs how each coefficient may be read.

  • Firm (green). Coral, depth and max relief are significant at every spacing in every one of the seven years, never flip sign, and move by less than 0.13 log-odds at their worst. They have fine-scale texture no smooth background can imitate, so the spatial field cannot take them. These are the coefficients the chapter reports.
  • Steady under spacing, unsettled between years (blue). None of these flips sign because of the lattice — offshore ratio does so in one year of seven, the rest never. Their instability is between years, which is a different question from spatial confounding and is treated as one. Nutrient · between is the strongest of them, holding its sign in all seven years and reaching significance at every spacing in five.
  • Never separated from zero at every spacing (amber). The three within-lagoon smooth terms are significant at no spacing in any year. Herbivore biomass is the same in five of seven years; it reaches p < 0.05 at the adopted 100 m spacing in 2022 and at three of four spacings in 2023, both small (+0.4 to +1.1 percentage points) and both on the late, thin fish-survey subset. That is not a consistent within-year locator, and it is not one of the three the chapter reports. Distance to pass · within has the widest swing in the table, 0.548, without ever being distinguishable from zero — which is the point.

One fit of the twenty-eight does not exist. 2022 at 75 m returns missing standard errors on the lagoon-grouped field and is therefore not recorded — the sensitivity refits are pinned to that field on purpose, since letting one fall back to a weaker spatial structure would compare a spatial model with a non-spatial one. Retried directly, it fails on the lagoon field, fails again on the island field, and only succeeds with the spatial term removed altogether. 2022 is the year with the fewest rows over the fewest lagoons, and at 75 m its six lagoons are asked for 137 knots; there is not enough data to pin the spatial variance down. It is a real limit, not a transient failure, and 2022 is judged on its other three spacings.

100 m is adopted as the point that still captures genuine broad structure without the field tracing the smooth predictors outright, and because it sits inside the stable region rather than at either edge of the range tested. All four are refitted and reported, so the choice is shown to be immaterial for the predictors this chapter actually rests on, rather than asserted to be. That sensitivity is the evidence for F2 rather than a side check.

The risk that remains

The lagoon-grouped field may still not converge in the thinnest years. Fitting a separate field per lagoon asks more of a thin lagoon-year than one island-wide field does, and the table above says which years those are: 2021 and 2022 carry six lagoons apiece. Knots make this much less likely — 2019 fitted in 0.08 min with no fallback — but the fallback is retained: an island-wide field with the range fixed short rather than estimated, reaching the same goal by a blunter route. Any year that falls back is reported as such.

1.5 · Three issues that survive the refit

These are properties of the data and the design, not of any particular fit, so changing the likelihood and the spatial term did not remove them. Each one still constrains how a coefficient in §2 may be worded, and each is referenced from the predictor table above.

F1 · Coral shares the response’s denominator, so its magnitude is the result

Response and predictor are both divided by Algae + Coral + HardSub. It is tempting to dismiss the negative coefficient as arithmetic, but that is too strong — and the algebra says why. With shares a + c + h = 1, the slope of algae share on coral share is −1 − cov(h,c)/var(c), which pins two interpretable endpoints:

  • β = 0 — the space coral does not hold is bare hard substrate. Algae’s share does not move at all.
  • β = −1 — the space coral does not hold is algae. Hard substrate is constant.

So zero is a genuinely possible outcome, and a significant negative does tell you algae occupies some of what coral does not. What is fixed by construction is the ceiling at −1, not the value. The current ordered-Beta fits, converted by the exact average-marginal-effect rule in §1.4, put it here:

Yearlog-odds / 2 SDMean algae shareExact AME, percentage points
2018-0.26917.4 %-3.0
2019-0.57911.9 %-4.6
2020*-0.62920.5 %-7.4
2021-0.77617.0 %-7.9
2022-0.69812.7 %-5.7
2023-0.48110.0 %-3.4
2024-0.55812.5 %-4.8

Percentage points of algae share per 2 SD of coral share, from the primary fits. *2020 is the Sep–Oct season and is excluded from the median.

The median effect is -4.7 percentage points per 2 SD. On the 2019 fit that is −4.6 points: moving a grid 2 SD up in coral takes its algae share from 11.9 % to 7.3 % of hard bottom. A real tradeoff in the predicted direction, but still far closer to the “coral’s space goes bare” end than to the “algae takes it” end — most of what coral does not hold is hard substrate, not algae.

The obligation this creates: report coral as a magnitude in share units, never as “strongest support for competition for space”. The defensible wording is where there is less coral there is somewhat more algae on the hard bottom, though most of the space coral does not hold is bare rather than algal.

F2 · A spatial field can compete with the smooth predictors, and Moran’s I cannot detect it

The split did not make this go away. It showed which half of each variable the competition was eating. That is a different — and more useful — statement than “problem solved.”

The original diagnosis is still the right one, and it is measured rather than suspected. Comparing the archived lagoon-only lmer against the island-wide spatial fit, and recovering standard errors from the estimates and p-values, separates two very different things a spatial field can be doing:

Predictor★ lmer★ spatialestimate

ratio		What the spatial term did

Offshore ratio (shore→crest)7/72/70.962.72×estimate intact, precision lost
% MPA2/70/71.151.99×estimate intact, precision lost
Depth (old coding; − = deeper)7/77/70.901.63×estimate intact, precision lost

Ratios are spatial ÷ lmer, median across the 7 previous fits. Row labels use the old variable coding, including depth as raw bathymetry, since that is what these fits used; the refit flips depth. % MPA and spear appear because they were in the old primary model. An estimate ratio near 1 with a large SE ratio means the coefficient did not move — only its precision did.

The four smooth spatial fields lost a factor of 2–3 in precision while their point estimates stayed put. Offshore ratio is the clearest case: significant in 7 of 7 years under lmer, 2 of 7 with the field, estimate essentially unchanged (ratio 0.96). Distance to pass, nutrient and %MPA behaved the same way. That is variance inflation from a random field competing for the same broad-scale variation — not the spatial term explaining those predictors away. Coral was untouched (SE ratio 0.97) because coral is patchy at fine scale and does not resemble anything the field wants to absorb.

Two changes were made to contain it, and they do different jobs. Grouping the field within lagoon stops it from correlating Haumi with Maharepa, so it can no longer imitate an island-wide surface. Splitting each smooth predictor into a lagoon mean and a within-lagoon deviation then asks the two questions of two different columns, so the remaining competition has only one half left to land on.

What is no longer a problem. The between-lagoon halves cannot be absorbed by a field that is estimated separately inside each lagoon — a within-lagoon field never sees a contrast that is constant inside the lagoon. That is why those three _btw coefficients never flip sign across knot spacings in any year, and why nutrient · between is significant at every spacing in five years of seven. The old island-wide competition is gone for that half.

What is still a problem. The within-lagoon halves vary over a few hundred metres inside a lagoon, which is exactly the scale the grouped field is now free to use. A neighbour correlation of 0.99 means a grid’s nutrient (or MPA, or distance to pass) is almost the same as its neighbours’ — and “nearby grids look alike” is also the only thing a spatial field knows how to say. The two are asking the same question of the same leftover variation, so the _wth coefficients are the ones that move when the knot spacing changes and the ones that never separate from zero. The split did not invent that null; it stopped a real lagoon-scale association from being averaged into it.

Moran’s I still cannot tell these two situations apart, which is why it is no longer the check this document relies on. After the old field was fitted, residual Moran’s I was −0.088 to −0.117 with p = 1.000000 in every year, against an expectation of about −0.0004. That was read as success. It is better read as an artifact: Moran’s I on conditional residuals of a fitted spatial field always overshoots negative, because the field has absorbed the autocorrelation and some of the signal with it. The statistic cannot tell a well-specified field from an over-smoothing one. The checks that can are the neighbour-correlation plot, the knot-spacing sensitivity, and the fitted range — all three of which are now in the document.

Which predictors are at risk is not a judgement call — it can be measured directly. A spatial field can only absorb a predictor that looks like a spatial field. So for each predictor, correlate a grid’s value against the mean of its neighbours within 100 m, computed within lagoon so lagoon identity cannot inflate it. A predictor near r = 1 carries the same value as its surroundings, which is precisely the information the field encodes:

Every survey year, all nine predictors. The dot is the mean across years and the bar is the full range, which is narrow — this is a property of the variables, not of one year.

The split is bimodal with nothing in between: the roughest “absorbed” predictor never falls below r = 0.977 in any year and the smoothest “identified” one never rises above 0.917, so the shaded gap is genuinely empty. Distance to pass, nutrient and MPA sit at 0.99–1.00; they are smooth surfaces, and against a spatial field they carry almost no information of their own. Coral, relief, VRM and herbivore biomass sit at 0.50–0.67, patchy enough that no smooth field can imitate them. Depth at 0.85 is the one genuine intermediate, which is why it survives but should be read with the spatial term in mind.

The exception is offshore ratio at r = 0.98, which is smooth enough to be at risk but is significant at all four spacings in 2019 nonetheless. Smoothness raises the risk of being absorbed; it does not guarantee it, and it is not a rule for discarding predictors. Offshore ratio fails a different test: it is significantly negative at all four spacings in 2019 (−0.46 to −0.63) and significantly positive at all four in 2021 (+0.23 to +0.37). A reversal with both ends significant is a between-year problem, not a spatial one, and is treated under that heading.

So the wording constraint is now specific rather than blanket. The between-lagoon components of nutrient, MPA and distance to pass are reported by the year models but are not tested by them — their honest sample size is eleven lagoons. The within-lagoon components are a spatial null: they never separate from zero, and the field is the reason. Neither half should be written up as a grid-scale nutrient, MPA or pass effect.

F3 · Relief and VRM are not separately identifiable

maxRel and VRM correlate at r = 0.83 on the rows the models see, which means their two coefficients cannot be separated by these data. That alone explains why VRM is unsettled across years while max relief is firm, without invoking any real change in rugosity. Nutrient and distance to pass correlate at r = −0.56, a milder version of the same problem.

The VIF reported previously was computed on a stacked ordinary design that ignored the spatial and random-effect structure, so it understates the true inflation rather than bounding it.

The obligation this creates: any claim about seabed complexity belongs to the pair, not to one member of it. The joint test is significant in all seven years, and VRM becomes a “finding” the moment max relief is dropped — which is the demonstration, not a second result. See §2.4. Neither variable is dropped from the primary model — the constraint is on the wording, not the specification.

The point of a register is that a reader can see the full set that was tried, not only the ones that happened to agree with the reported result. Sign and significance are stable: the two likelihoods agree on sign for 82 of 84 coefficients and on significance for 78 of 84. Every one of the six significance disagreements falls on distance to pass or nutrient — predictors already flagged in §1.3 as unable to support a claim — so none of them touches a reported finding.

But the magnitudes are not stable, and in a consistent direction. The Smithson–Verkuilen nudge attenuates the coral coefficient in every single year:

The nudge shifts exact zeros a little way off the boundary, which compresses the response and flattens the slope against it. That the bias runs one way in all seven years, and reaches 4.0 SE in 2022, is the practical case for ordered Beta over the nudge: the two agree about whether coral matters, but not about how much, and the effect size is what gets quoted.

sensitivityS5 — which spatial structure each fit actually ended up with

The lagoon-grouped field is tried first in every fit. Where a year is too thin to support it the model steps down to a single island-wide field, and then to no spatial term. This is reported per fit rather than hidden, because a coefficient from a year with no spatial term is not comparable to one from a year that carried the full field.

The paired families step down more often because they run on smaller subsets, but in every case both arms move together, so no pair is ever comparing two different specifications.

sensitivityS6 — the herbivore sampling footprint does bite in the late years

Yes, this is a problem — but not the problem the one-line maximum implies. Family A is fitted on the fish-surveyed grids by construction (herbivore is never imputed). Family B exists to ask whether that deletion changes the geography. The control years confirm the machinery works: where coverage is 98–100 %, restoring the missing grids moves nothing (max 0.17 SD). Where coverage falls to 37–43 %, something real moves. The question is what.

2022 and 2023 are the years that matter for the chapter. Depth — one of the three coefficients §2 reports — shifts by 2.5 and 2.4 of its own standard error when the unsurveyed grids come back in (log-odds −1.25 vs −1.04 in 2022; −1.01 vs −0.90 in 2023). The sign never changes and the effect stays large, so the finding deeper grids hold less algae is not an artefact of the fish-survey map. The magnitude in those two years is: family A’s late-year depth coefficients describe the fish-surveyed slice, which is 37–43 % of the reef and sits further offshore, and they should not be pooled with 2018–2021 as if they were the same estimand.

The 6.7 SD in 2024 is not a geography problem. It is the within-lagoon MPA term, which is already a spatial null and is never reported as a finding. That pair also had to drop the spatial field entirely (S5), so 2024’s magnitude should not be quoted from either arm. Coral and max relief keep their sign in every pair; their late-year shifts stay below 2 SD.

sensitivityS9 — the two years where MPA cannot be estimated at all

In 2021 and 2022 the within-lagoon MPA term is exactly zero for every row: within the fished-and-surveyed subset those years, every lagoon is either wholly inside or wholly outside the reserve. There is no contrast to estimate, so the model is rank deficient and the year fails outright.

Rather than lose two years, the term is dropped for those two fits and the fact is recorded in fishing_coverage under dropped_terms. The honest statement is not “MPA had no effect in 2021–2022” but “those years contain no within-lagoon MPA comparison to make”. The guard is general and always reports what it removed — it never drops a term silently.

sensitivityS10 — residual diagnostics, including the one test that fails

Two of the three DHARMa tests are clean in all seven years. Dispersion is fine, which matters because the model estimates it from photo count rather than assuming it. Zero-inflation is fine, which is the direct check that ordered Beta is handling the exact zeros properly and no separate zero-inflation component is needed.

The uniformity test is rejected in every year, and this should be stated plainly rather than buried. The reason it is not treated as fatal is the size of the departure: the KS statistic runs 0.030–0.066, meaning the residual distribution sits within about three to seven percentage points of uniform. At n = 1,379–3,895 a KS test detects deviations far too small to distort a coefficient, which is a well-known property of goodness-of-fit tests at large n. The check that would actually matter for these estimates — dispersion — passes.

What is deliberately not in this register

Three things a reader might expect to find here are absent, on purpose:

  • Temperature. Not fitted in the year models at all. Within-year, between-site variation is negligible against between-year variation, so it is collinear with lagoon identity — see §1.2.
  • Spear density in the primary model. Excluded from families A and B rather than tested there: 61.7 % of its values were imputed zeros, and the no-data flag predicted algae better than the real measurements did. It is tested in family C on measured grids only.
  • Grid resolution. Fixed at 10 × 10 m throughout. Knot spacing (S1) varies the resolution of the spatial field, not of the data.

2 · Results

The result, in one paragraph

Three predictors survive every check, and they are the same three every year. On the hard bottom, algae is lower where coral is higher, lower where it is deeper, and higher where relief is greater — each significant after Benjamini–Hochberg correction in all seven years, with the sign never once reversing. Nothing else in the model manages that. Fishing pressure and the within-lagoon components of nutrient, MPA and distance to pass are not distinguishable from zero in any year. Herbivore biomass reaches BH significance in 2022 and 2023 only, both small (+1.1 and +0.4 percentage points) and both on the late fish-survey subset; the sign is not stable across the series, so it is not a finding. The between-lagoon components are large and often significant, but they rest on eleven lagoons and cannot be read as grid-scale effects.

All seven models converged on the full lagoon-grouped spatial field with no fallbacks, and the previous Gaussian analysis is preserved unaltered in chapter2_q1_by_year_lmer_no_fringing.html.

Depth is the largest effect in the model, worth −5.5 to −10.7 percentage points in the six May–Jun years (−13.3 in the Sep–Oct 2020 season), against a mean share of 10–20 %. Coral runs −3.0 to −7.9 and max relief +1.3 to +3.3. All three are stable in sign and comparable in magnitude across seven years, which is the strongest claim this design can support.

The between-lagoon numbers are not comparable to these and must not be read as if they were. Nutrient · between reaches +45.8 percentage points in 2021, which is larger than the mean share itself. That is what happens when 2 SD of a lagoon-level variable spans most of the island: it is a contrast between whole lagoons, estimated on eleven of them, not an effect you could produce by changing anything at a grid. See §1.2 for why it stays in the model anyway.

What the fitted spatial range tells you

The field settles at 158 to 432 m in six of the seven years, with 2024 the exception at 1,069 m. The range is the distance at which two grids inside the same lagoon stop sharing leftover algae that the named predictors did not explain. Two things follow, and they point in opposite directions, which is why both are stated.

It vindicates the knot choice. A field with a 158 m range needs a lattice finer than that to be resolved, and 100 m is. Every year’s range is 1.6 to 10.7 times the knot spacing, so the lattice is not the thing limiting what the field can represent.

It also says, in metres, where the leftover pattern lives. Think of the named predictors as having already taken every bit of algae they can claim. What is left — currents, sediment, a boat track, a patch of disturbance the model has no column for — is what the spatial field is for. A range of a few hundred metres means: two grids 200 m apart inside one lagoon still share some of that leftover; two grids in different lagoons do not, except through the lagoon intercept. That is local structure. It is not an island-wide trend — so the field is not quietly absorbing broad gradients. But it is operating at exactly the scale the within-lagoon components of the smooth predictors vary at, which is consistent with those being the terms that move under respecification and never separate from zero. The field and those three terms are asking the same question of the same variation. See F2.

2.2 · Herbivore footprint check — family B

Fourteen fits, one pair per year: the same model on all rows and then on the fish-surveyed subset only. This is a diagnostic, not a result. It asks one question — does dropping the grids without a fish survey change the geography coefficients? — because family A is fitted on that subset by construction.

Across all seven pairs. “Shift” is the change in the coefficient between the two arms, in log-odds. The figure shows the same contrast as a z-score; the orange band is the low-coverage years.

The finding survives the deletion; the late-year magnitude of depth does not

Every geography coefficient keeps its sign in all seven pairs. Coral, depth and max relief are never reversed by restoring the unsurveyed grids. That is the claim that matters for the chapter: family A is not discovering a pattern that only exists on the fish-survey map.

The design of the check is what makes that readable. In 2018–2021 coverage is 98.1 to 99.8 %, so the two arms are almost the same rows and agreement is expected — those years are the control that shows the machinery works. The test has teeth in 2022–2024, where coverage falls to 36.8–43.2 %.

And there the magnitude of depth does move, by 2.4 to 2.5 of its own standard error. That is a problem for quoting a single late-year depth effect as if it described the whole reef, and it is not a problem for the sign. Family A in 2022–2023 is estimated on the fish-surveyed slice, which sits further offshore than the grids the ROV added; those two years’ depth coefficients should be reported as such, not averaged with 2018–2021. The 6.7 SD figure in the S6 one-liner is the 2024 within-lagoon MPA term on a pair that had no spatial field, and it is not a finding. Detail in §1.6 / S6.

Spear coefficient in log-odds per 2 SD. q is Benjamini–Hochberg across years.

No detectable fishing signal, and MPA does not notice spear arriving

Spear density is not distinguishable from zero in any of the seven years. Raw p runs 0.126 to 0.968 and no q-value comes near 0.05; the coefficients are small in both directions (−0.106 to +0.080) with standard errors as large or larger. This is a null, and it is reported as one.

Adding spear moves the MPA coefficient by at most 0.049 log-odds, and in three of five comparable years by less than 0.005. Whatever MPA is picking up in these models, it is not standing in for fishing effort — which is the specific confound this pair was built to test. The measured correlation between MPA and spear density is |r| ≤ 0.073 in every year, so the two are close to orthogonal in this data.

Two years are missing an MPA comparison: in 2021 and 2022 the within-lagoon MPA term has no variation left inside the surviving lagoons and is dropped automatically, which the pipeline logs rather than silently absorbing. Those years still test spear; they just cannot speak to MPA.

The honest limit is power. These fits run on 504 to 1,607 rows across five to nine lagoons, so a small fishing effect would not be detected here. The result is no evidence of an effect, not evidence of no effect.

2.4 · Diagnostics

Every primary fit was checked with DHARMa simulated residuals. The dispersion and zero-inflation tests are in the table in §2.1; both pass in all seven years, which is the specific reassurance ordered Beta was adopted to obtain.

The KS test is significant in all seven years, and this is expected

The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test on the simulated residuals returns p < 0.05 in every year. Left unexplained that looks alarming, so: at n = 1,379 to 3,895 a KS test has enough power to detect departures from uniformity far too small to affect any coefficient, and it will reject for essentially any real dataset. The informative tests are the ones aimed at specific failures the model could plausibly have:

  • Dispersion: ratios 0.95 to 1.54, none significant (smallest p = 0.11). The dispformula term is doing its job.
  • Zero-inflation: ratios 0.93 to 1.12, none significant (smallest p = 0.48). The ordered Beta accounts for the exact zeros without a separate zero-inflation component, which is precisely the claim it was chosen on and the reason no ziformula is fitted.

Neither of those would pass automatically, and both were live possibilities before the refit. They are the checks that carry information; the KS result is not.

S11 · Within-lagoon residual variograms

The fitted range is one number per year. A number can hide a field that reports a plausible range while still leaving structure at 20–50 m that it never absorbed. The variogram is the check that a range cannot fake: for every pair of grids inside the same lagoon, bin by separation and compute the semivariance of the DHARMa residuals, then divide by the residual variance so 1.0 means no leftover structure.

Blue lines are individual lagoons; the dark line is pair-weighted across lagoons. The dashed grey line is 1.0. The dotted orange line is the 100 m knot spacing. A reading below 1 at short lags is leftover positive autocorrelation.

Year~12 m~38 m~88 mPlateau (500–1,500 m)
20180.410.470.510.64
20190.530.590.680.78
20200.560.660.760.99
20210.570.650.680.95
20220.650.740.840.96
20230.460.510.590.78
20240.400.460.510.76

There is leftover structure inside 50 m, in every year

At ~12 m the relative semivariance is 0.40 to 0.65. Neighbouring 10 m grids still look more alike than a well-absorbed field would leave them. That is expected rather than alarming: the spatial term is anchored on a 100 m lattice, so it is not being asked to resolve a 10–50 m pattern, and it does not. By ~500 m most years have drifted up toward 1, which is consistent with the fitted ranges of 158–432 m.

What this does and does not threaten. Leftover short-range correlation can make standard errors a little optimistic. It does not invent a sign. Coral, depth and max relief have z-scores far larger than that optimism could account for, and they survive every other respecification in the register. The terms that would be most exposed to leftover local structure are the three within-lagoon smooth components, and those are already reported as nulls. The honest sentence is: the field is doing the job it was given at the scale it was given; it is not a complete model of every metre of leftover algae.

The pattern is the same every year: max relief is significant whether VRM is in the model or not; VRM is usually a null beside it and becomes a finding the moment max relief is dropped. That is what r = 0.83 looks like in a coefficient table. A claim about seabed complexity belongs to the pair. The wording algae is higher where relief is greater is the defensible one; max relief matters and VRM does not is not, because the second half of that sentence is an artefact of which member of the pair was left in.

S13 · Photo threshold, and whether dispersion is still needed

The adopted floor is 20 photographs. Refitting at 5 and at 30, and again at 20 with dispformula = ~ 1, asks whether that judgement moves the answer. Shifts are in standard-error units of the adopted fit. A year is dropped from an arm when that arm could not hold the same spatial field as the adopted model, so a fallback is not counted as a threshold effect.

Arm vs adopted 20Median shift (SE)Max shiftSign flipsSignificance changesFirm three, max SE
threshold 50.1572.1962/8462.196
threshold 300.1451.0633/7221.063
no dispformula0.0470.5061/7220.506

threshold 30 drops 2020 (spatial field fell back, so the shift is not a threshold effect); no dispformula drops 2022 (spatial field fell back, so the shift is not a threshold effect). Dispersion LRT against a constant-dispformula model is significant in 7 of 7 years, so the effort term is still earning its keep at a 128-fold range.

Twenty is not doing hidden work. The firm three never reverse sign at either neighbouring floor. Dropping the effort-dispersion term moves them by half a standard error at most, and a likelihood-ratio test still wants the term in every year, so dispformula = ~ log(n_photos) stays. The one year that could not support a spatial field at 30 photos is 2020 — already the flagged Sep–Oct season — and it is excluded from that row rather than allowed to inflate the shift.

2.5 · Narrow scope — within lagoon, and paired grids

Family A mixes lagoons. The Mundlak split handles that for the smooth three, but coral, depth and max relief are not split. Two further checks ask whether those three survive when lagoon identity and (separately) the exact grid set are locked down. Both use the locked rules — ordered Beta, ≥ 20 photos, no Ch1 filter, no spear — and fit only the firm three, so the row set is every photographed grid, not the fish-surveyed subset.

Within each lagoon, each year

One model per lagoon-year with enough rows (n ≥ 50). No lagoon random intercept — it would be unidentified — and a within-lagoon spatial field when it converges. Coefficients sit on the same year-wide Gelman 2-SD scale as family A.

Depth is a within-lagoon fact; coral and relief usually are

Depth is negative in every one of the 58 fitted lagoon-years, and BH-significant in 57. That is the cleanest confirmation this design can give: the island-wide depth coefficient is not an artefact of which lagoons were surveyed which year.

Coral is negative in 45 of 58, max relief positive in 51 of 58. The minority flips are real and should be stated — a few lagoon-years run the other way — but the dominant sign matches family A, and most of those fits are BH-significant. The firm three are not being carried by lagoon composition.

Same grids, consecutive years

For each lagoon and each consecutive year-pair, keep only grid_IDs usable in both years and fit the firm three twice on that fixed map. 23 of 40 lagoon-pairs had at least 50 overlapping grids; the rest are thin lagoons or years with little resurvey overlap, and are recorded as skips rather than forced.

Holding the map fixed does not overturn the firm three

Depth keeps its sign in every paired comparison (23 of 23). Coral flips once; max relief flips twice. Magnitude can move — depth shifts by more than 2 SE in six pairs — but the direction does not. So the year-to-year instability that worried the chapter is not being driven by the survey footprint wandering onto different reef; on the cells that were resurveyed, the same relationships hold.

Taken with family B (fish-survey footprint within a year) and this section (locked map across years), the sampling concern is bounded: late-year depth magnitude should still be quoted with the fish-survey restriction in mind (§2.2), but the sign of the firm three is not a sampling artefact.

Same rules, different formula — and 2020

Narrow scope is a confirmation that the firm three survive when lagoon (and map) are locked. It is not a slice of the full primary model, and it does not re-test herbivore, offshore, VRM, or the nutrient / MPA / pass halves. Those stay at whatever family A said.

2.6 · What has been verified, and what this design cannot push further

Family A is the reported model. Everything else exists to ask whether those three coefficients are an artefact of a specification, a row set, or a spatial field. This is the full set that was asked.

CheckWhat it asked of the firm three What it showed
S2 likelihood Gaussian / squeezed Beta / ordered Beta Signs agree. Magnitudes do not: the squeeze attenuates coral in every year (up to 4.0 SE). Ordered Beta is kept because the effect size is the claim.
S1 knot spacing 150 / 100 / 75 / 50 m Significant at every spacing in every year; never flip; worst move 0.13 log-odds.
S3 / S4 smooth design Pooled vs split vs drop the three smooths Firm three move by at most 0.287 SE. The split is for interpretability, not confounding control.
S13 photo threshold Floor at 5 / 20 / 30, and dispformula dropped Signs never reverse. Dropping dispersion moves them by at most 0.51 SE; the effort term stays.
S12 relief pair Joint {maxRel, VRM} and drop-one Joint test 7/7. The pair is the finding; VRM alone is not.
S6 / B fish-survey footprint All photographed grids vs the fish-surveyed subset Signs hold. Late-year depth magnitude moves 2.4–2.5 SE and must be quoted as the fish-surveyed slice.
S5 spatial structure Lagoon field → island → none Family A held the lagoon field in all seven years. No fallback on a headline fit.
S10 / S11 residuals DHARMa + within-lagoon variograms Dispersion and zero-inflation pass. KS rejects at this n, as expected. Leftover structure inside 50 m is real and expected of a 100 m lattice; it does not invent a sign.
S14 within lagoon One fit per lagoon-year, firm three only, full photo map Depth negative in 58/58 (49/49 May–Jun). Coral and relief usually match family A.
S15 paired grids Same grid_IDs, consecutive years Depth same sign in 23/23 (21/21 May–Jun). Coral flips once; relief twice.

The firm three have been pushed as far as this design can push them

Every specification that could have overturned coral, depth or max relief was run. None did, on sign. The one magnitude caveat that survives is late-year depth under the fish-survey footprint (S6). The one residual caveat that survives is leftover 10–50 m structure the 100 m field is not asked to absorb (S11). Neither invents the finding.

Three things were not done, on purpose:

  • The other predictors inside one lagoon. The _btw halves are constant there. Herbivore would throw away the photo map. This is not a gap in verifying the firm three; it would make the check worse at its job.
  • Temperature, or any other time-varying covariate, in these year models. Within-year, between-site heat variation is negligible against between-year variation, so it is collinear with lagoon identity. That question is a different analysis.
  • A finer spatial lattice, or a different grid size. 50 m already sits in the S1 set; the firm three do not move. The leftover short-lag pattern would need a different model class, and that class is not required to trust these signs.

What remains is wording, not verification. Coral is a composition split whose magnitude is the result (F1). The within-lagoon smooths are a spatial null (F2). Relief and VRM are one pair (F3). 2020 is a different season. Between-lagoon coefficients rest on eleven lagoons. Family C is a scoped null with limited power. Those constraints travel with the result; they are not unfinished checks.
